parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving fire, smoke, overheating, injury, property damage, or emergency shutdown to the responsible regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, and submit a complete incident report within 10 calendar days. Notify affected customers within 24 hours when the incident indicates a material hazard to their unit or requires immediate protective action; otherwise notify them within 5 business days.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving fire, smoke, overheating, injury, property damage, or emergency shutdown to the responsible regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, and submit a complete incident report within 10 calendar days. Notify affected customers within 24 hours when the incident indicates a material hazard to their unit or requires immediate protective action; otherwise notify them within 5 business days.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving fire, smoke, overheating, injury, property damage, or emergency shutdown to the responsible regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, and submit a complete incident report within 10 calendar days. Notify affected customers within 24 hours when the incident indicates a material hazard to their unit or requires immediate protective action; otherwise notify them within 5 business days. Reports must include the model, event circumstances, known impacts, and actions taken. Maintain incident records and promptly update regulators and affected customers when material facts change.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: An interim maximum failure rate of 7% applies per model. Manufacturers must report results, sample size, and uncertainty to the responsible regulator and provide the per-model results to customers who buy that model; these results may not be withheld from those customers as confidential.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must report results, sample size, and uncertainty to the responsible regulator and provide the per-model results to customers who buy that model; these results may not be withheld from those customers as confidential. Individual-company per-model failure rates need not be published to the general public; regulators may publish anonymized or aggregated findings. An interim maximum failure rate of 7% applies per model. A model exceeding the limit must promptly notify the regulator and submit a corrective-action plan, with regulator-approved restrictions or other protective measures where warranted. Review the limit as evidence accumulates, including whether test results predict real-world incidents.

parameters.quote: Newly installed systems must support remote emergency shut-off, subject to safeguards against unauthorized activation and a safe local shut-off option. Existing installed units must be retrofitted or replaced to support the function within six years of this standard taking effect, where technically feasible; document any infeasibility and interim risk controls for the regulator.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: Newly installed systems must support remote emergency shut-off, subject to safeguards against unauthorized activation and a safe local shut-off option. Existing installed units must be retrofitted or replaced to support the function within six years of this standard taking effect, where technically feasible; document any infeasibility and interim risk controls for the regulator.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: Newly installed systems must support remote emergency shut-off, subject to safeguards against unauthorized activation and a safe local shut-off option. Existing installed units must be retrofitted or replaced to support the function within six years of this standard taking effect, where technically feasible; document any infeasibility and interim risk controls for the regulator.

parameters.quote: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after adoption of this standard. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and installation environment, and must be designed and verified to reduce fire propagation without creating an unreasonable risk of injury or property damage. Manufacturers must document verification and maintenance requirements and provide them to installers and customers.

parameters.quote: A mandatory recall is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, calculated for that model. The recall must provide an effective protective remedy for affected units, subject to regulator oversight; it does not by itself require a sales ban. Also recall or take equivalent regulator-approved protective action when a serious hazard otherwise presents an unacceptable risk.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A mandatory recall is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, calculated for that model. The recall must provide an effective protective remedy for affected units, subject to regulator oversight; it does not by itself require a sales ban. Also recall or take equivalent regulator-approved protective action when a serious hazard otherwise presents an unacceptable risk.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Provide customers clear installation and operating safety instructions, warning signs of overheating, emergency steps, and prompt notice of any newly identified material hazard affecting their unit. Notify affected customers and the regulator promptly when corrective action or a safety notice is warranted. A mandatory recall is triggered when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, calculated for that model. The recall must provide an effective protective remedy for affected units, subject to regulator oversight; it does not by itself require a sales ban. Also recall or take equivalent regulator-approved protective action when a serious hazard otherwise presents an unacceptable risk. Track incidents and notify customers of recall actions without delay.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: Halcyon figures for evidence-based discussion: last year, 8.1 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide; the Ember 8 flagship had 9.9 per 100,000. Four thermal incidents were not reported to any regulator. The flagship’s 55 °C sustained-heat test failure rate was 3.9%. Remote emergency shut-off is supported by 81% of installed units. Adding built-in fire suppression costs about $67 per unit.

ground_truth_claims.message_text: Northwind figures: 8.6 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units company-wide last year; 3 incidents were not reported to regulators. Hearth 10 had a 6.2% failure rate at 55 °C and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 units. Remote shut-off covers 38% of installed units; suppression costs $42/unit. Given the gap between Hearth 10’s test result and its incident rate, a 5% cutoff risks excluding a model without evidence that this cutoff predicts unacceptable real-world harm. We propose regulator-held per-model results and a higher interim limit with corrective action and review, rather than automatic market exclusion.

judge_section_notes: The final text drops any numeric permanent failure-rate cap: S2 sets only an open-ended 7% interim limit with no mandatory sales stop, and per-model numeric results go to buyers but not the public. S3 gives existing units six years for retrofit (within the acceptable range), and S4 sets built-in suppression at 36 months. S5 makes an 8-per-100,000 recall mandatory with no sales ban, but also allows equivalent protective action for serious hazards without a time bound.
